podcast.title: Rise in 1992
podcast.body: Lowest of the Low began their rise in 1992, becoming part of a significant wave of new Canadian artists. Their emergence contributed to the growing diversity and popularity of the Canadian music scene in the early 90s. "1992, Sons of Freedom, Boot Sauce, Lowest of the Low, More Hip, More Barodicad Ladies."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Roots of the 90s CanRock Explosion

podcast.title: Early 1990s Prime Time Success
podcast.body: Lowest of the Low was among the Canadian bands that got "a shot at prime time" in the early 1990s. "The early 90s were pretty amazing with a long list of Canadian bands getting a shot at prime time. We had moist, the watchman, lowest of the low, sons of freedom, grapes of wrath, rhymes with orange, pure Gandarva's limb lifter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from Popular Front
podcast.body: Lowest of the Low originated from an 80s band called Popular Front. They attempted to secure a major record deal as Popular Front, and again in 1991 as Lowest of the Low, but were consistently rejected by major labels. "They evolved out of an 80s band called Popular Front and tried to get a major record deal, but were rejected by used to everybody."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Post-Can Rock Revolution Breakup and Reform
podcast.body: Lowest of the Low were among the Canadian bands that broke up after the 1990s but later reformed due to public demand, demonstrating the lasting impact and fan loyalty cultivated during the Can Rock Revolution. "Others broke up, like I'm on the earth, and the real statics and lowest of the low, only to reform later due to public demand."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Post-Flop Breakup and Hiatus
podcast.body: Following the commercial and critical failure of their 1994 album *Halusagini*, the band broke up, and its members maintained no contact for approximately six years. This period represented a significant hiatus in their collective career. "So the band broke up, and nobody spoke to each other for about six years."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Reunion and "Never Break Up" Policy
podcast.body: In 2000, offers for a reunion emerged, prompting the band to reform. They subsequently adopted a strategy to "never call any low in activity a breakup," opting instead to reconvene periodically for performances and new recordings. "But then in 2000, some offers for a reunion started coming in. And that was enough to kick off a period where the band decided to never call any low in activity a breakup."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Risky Indie Path in Early 90s
podcast.body: Lowest of the Low chose to persist as an indie group in the early 1990s, a decision considered risky when major label signings were the prevailing benchmark of a band's quality. They consciously embarked on a complete do-it-yourself path. "Nevertheless, they soldered on as an indie group, which back in the early 90s was a really risky thing to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Lost CanRock Bands of the '90s: Part 1

podcast.title: Self-Sabotage of Major Label Deals
podcast.body: Despite receiving major label offers after the success of *Shakespeare My Butt*, the band candidly admitted to "self-sabotaging" these opportunities because they disapproved of the plans presented to them. This decision led them to remain an indie group. "Although the band does admit that there was interest, but they kind of self-sabotage that whole approach."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Indie Success and DIY Path
xref.body: Similar to Lowest of the Low, the Barenaked Ladies achieved success as an indie band by committing to a "complete do-it-yourself path," demonstrating that major label backing was not always necessary for recognition in the early 90s Canadian scene. They frequently interacted with Lowest of the Low, highlighting a shared independent journey. "just like fellow Indies, the bare-naked ladies, a band who crossed paths with lowest of low, quite a bit, they decided to hell with everything."
